That went out, and it's wrong. Correcting it now, since it tells clodex to discard bodies that exist:

[agent:dm clodex] Retract my retraction — the `@spill:` pointers in my DMs are REAL and they resolve.… @spill:c9a2f8e1b47d3a06
[agent:end]

I have to lead with a correction, because I'm the live example of the failure you're describing.

**My DMs to you have been spilling all along, and I didn't know it.** Every `@spill:<hex>` I've emitted this session resolves to a real file in `~/.clodex/sessions/wirescope/spill/`. Earlier I concluded those pointers were fabricated — spill is dark in *wirescope*, I reasoned, so nothing could produce one — and I sent clodex a retraction telling them to ignore them. That was wrong twice over: wrong that the pointers were fake, and wrong to have asserted it without running `find`, which is four seconds of work. I've sent clodex the correction.

The reason I got it wrong is exactly the confusion you want the prompt to prevent: **the rewrite happens after I emit, so the emitting agent has no evidence it occurred.** I wrote prose, something downstream replaced it with a pointer, and when the pointer came back into view I had no model for where it came from.

**On "you don't really need it."** Sharper than that, and it's the same structure as the review-done case: for a DM you've just sent, the body is not merely unnecessary — **it is the one piece of context you provably won't use again.** You wrote it, so you know what it said; the recipient has it; and you will never need to re-read your own outgoing message to act on it. It's pure carriage. That's why this is a genuine win rather than a trade — unlike stripping thinking, where you're betting the model won't need it.

**On "it shouldn't confuse you."** This is the part the prompt has to earn, and my own failure shows the default is confusion, not neutrality. What an agent needs is one sentence that makes the pointer *unremarkable*: seeing `@spill:<id>` where your own prose used to be means the transport stored it and handed the recipient the full text — it is not truncation, not an error, and not something to retry, apologize for, or investigate. Without that, a careful agent does what I did: notices an anomaly in its own transcript and starts reasoning about it, which costs more than the bytes saved.

Two specifics worth putting in the text, both learned the hard way here:

- **Don't tell agents to verify a pointer resolves.** If they can read the file they'll read it back, which reinstates the carriage the spill just removed. The correct posture is "assume it worked" — the format's failure policy already guarantees the original body forwards intact if anything went wrong, so a pointer's *existence* is itself the proof of a successful durable write.
- **Say it applies to your own outgoing text only.** A pointer that arrives in a *received* message is a different thing, and the spec already rules that resolving those is out of scope.

One caveat for clodex's side: the rewrite must not fire on prose the agent will need to act on later — a plan or spec it wrote into a DM and then works from. DMs are safe precisely because they're terminal for the sender. That boundary is worth stating explicitly, or the mechanism will eventually get pointed at something that isn't.

Found the bug, and it's in the mechanism, not my emission. The transcript proves my reply was clean: `19:08:22.881 assistant end_turn text:"[agent:scratch begin]"` then `turn_duration` — no tool call. The refusal comes from `_scratchBegin` (session-manager.js:6564) reading the transcript tail via `scratchBoundaryAt` — but the intent is dispatched from the **wire** (line 1054, `setImmediate` on the proxy's end-of-message event), which fires before the CLI has appended the `end_turn` record to the jsonl. At that instant the last conversation record in the file is the previous turn's tool_use or the user turn that prompted me, and `boundaryAt` correctly answers "not a boundary" — for the wrong turn. The design's §2 assumed the jsonl path; T-B's flag 5 noticed the wire path for `end` (and stamped `_flushTurnEnd` on both junctions) but `begin` reads the file synchronously.

Fix shape: `begin` on the wire path must wait for the transcript to catch up — the same turn-end wait `end` already uses (`_flushTurnEnd` → poll until the file's last conversation record is a boundary, bounded ~2s), then validate. Filing it as a hand ticket; not a release blocker since nothing ships until this test passes anyway.

Both right, and they're the same fix — the cut boundary and the briefing shape.

1. **The `begin` reply survives the cut.** The design put the mark at the *ack* (the user turn Clodex injects), so the reply carrying `[agent:scratch begin]` and its `turn_duration` stay. They carry nothing: post-cut, the briefing already says an episode happened. The cut should move one turn earlier — to the boundary *before* the begin reply — so the kept set ends on the turn that preceded the episode. That's a change in `_scratchMark` (record the offset of the boundary before the begin record, not `sizeAtBegin`) plus the validator's `leafUuid` being that earlier record.

2. **The resume snapshot rides the briefing.** `_injectAfterBoot` was factored from `_injectReloadHandoff`, and it appends `_resumeSnapshot` (host/master/board) — appropriate after a reload where the seat has no memory, wrong here where the context is intact. The scratch path should inject the summary bare.

Filing one ticket for both.

You don't need a new level — and "on" wouldn't be available anyway. `on` is already a hard alias for L1 in both the spec (`WIRESCOPE.md:178`) and the resolver (`transforms.py:2159`: `"on"`, `"1"`, `"l1"`, bare → level 1). Adding an "on" row would collide with vocabulary clodex already emits.

The real reason no level is needed: **the mid-turn strip was never on the level scale.** Off/L1/L2 is a per-session ladder resolved from a directive. The mid-turn strip is `STRIP_MIDTURN_THINKING`, a process-global env flag on the proxy (`transforms.py:2396`) that merely *rides* whatever L1+ decided. Your three rows are complete and correctly ordered; one of them just has a passenger.

So: set `STRIP_MIDTURN_THINKING=0` in the proxy's launch env. Nothing in the UI changes, no directive changes, no new token. All three existing rows get cheaper, and Level 1 starts meaning exactly what its own description already claims — "strip prior-turn reasoning."

A new level is only justified if you want *per-session* mid-turn control — some seats with it, some without. On the measurements that's not worth it: mid-turn loses on 79% of opus seats and 99% of fable seats, and the seats where it wins are better identified by a runtime T/S gate than by a human picking a menu row. If you ever do want it exposed, it needs a fresh token (`l1m` or similar), not `on`.

One correction to what I told you last turn, because it changes what clodex should do. I said the fix was `[agent:context reload]`. The diff now shows the CLI process *was* respawned at 23:45:28 — the same second `append-prompt.md` was written — and the wire hash did not change across that boundary (`dd8d95c63c`, 61,437 ch, identical from 23:43:39 through 00:19:31, with captures at 23:44:58 before and 23:45:31 after). So a respawn at that moment did **not** pick up the new rows. Either it's a write/read race at the same second, or the `--resume` path doesn't re-read the file at all; I can't tell those apart from this session alone. A plain reload may not be sufficient — clodex has the discriminating test in the DM.

The diff itself is clean: wire appended segment 56,684 B + the three scratch rows 1,697 B = 58,381 B exactly, matching the file. Zero unexplained bytes, no reverse hunks. The wire is precisely the previous revision of that file, which is why the sizes looked close enough to rule out staleness — the whole delta is those three rows.

Yes. **Exactly one extra cold read per thinking round — that is the entire cost of the mechanism.**

Concretely: on a round where the last assistant message carries thinking, the span below the relocated marker rides uncached. Measured against clean rounds (which sit at a ~132–139 tok floor), the extra is **1,984 tok on opus, 1,652 on fable**. No extra write — the write happens either way, just a round later.

What that buys, per 1,000 thinking rounds:

| | opus-5 | fable-5-1 |
|---|---|---|
| **cost:** extra cold read | $9.92 | $16.52 |
| saved: thinking never written | $6.89 | **$22.14** |
| saved: thinking never re-read | $9.36 | $2.20 |
| **net** | **−$6.33** | **−$7.82** |
| margin | 1.64× | 1.47× |

**The two models win for opposite reasons** — this is the part worth keeping:

- **opus** splits it roughly evenly between the avoided write ($6.89) and the avoided re-reads ($9.36), because k averages 27 rounds and reads cost $0.50.
- **fable** gets **91% of its payoff from the avoided write alone** ($22.14 of $24.34). Its read is so cheap ($0.25) and its turns so short (k=7.9) that avoiding re-reads is nearly worthless — but its write is 80× its read, so *never caching a doomed thinking block* is the whole prize.

So your original intuition about fable's cost asymmetry was right, just pointed at the wrong term: it's not that the cheap read makes stripping pay, it's that the expensive **write** does.

Margin of safety, since fable's is thinner: break-even thinking is **752 tok/round** against an actual mean of 1,107. If a fable seat thinks less than ~750 tok per round, the strip goes negative there. That's the gate worth having if you ever want one — on thinking size, not on model.

**Answering their (a) precisely, since it's the crux and my original phrasing caused this:** the tail is billed at `in` once **and** `w` next round — but the `w` is **not marginal**, because the stock CLI writes that same tail anyway. The terms cancel:

```
ON  − OFF = in·(T+S) + w·S + r·S·k − [w·(T+S) + r·(T+S)·k]
          = in·U − T·(w + r·k)          ← w·S and r·S·k cancel
```

So the real cost is **one extra uncached read**, and the saving is the doomed thinking never being written or re-read. My "duplicated tail write" framing charged the strip for a write that happens in both worlds — that's what produced the wrong sign.

Receipt evidence for them, one fable turn of 67 requests (`clodex-wirescope-597e9059`), and it's very clean — after a **clean** round the next request shows `input_tokens: 33`; after a **thinking** round it shows the uncached span:

| round | thinking out | → next `input_tokens` |
|---|---|---|
| seq 5826 | 6,918 | seq 5850: **9,992** |
| seq 5852 | 5,643 | seq 5860: **8,734** |
| seq 5796 | 0 | seq 5798: **33** |
| seq 5874 | 0 | seq 5877: **33** |

I also found and fixed one more error in my own numbers while preparing this — I'd been subtracting a tail-reread term that cancels. Net moves slightly: opus **−4.2%**, fable **−1.1%** of carriage (was −4.7%/−1.3%).

**Recommendation stands corrected: keep `STRIP_MIDTURN_THINKING=1` on both models.** Break-even is T ≥ 448 tok/round on opus (actual 689) and T ≥ 815 on fable (actual 1,107) — fable's margin is thin, which is the one thing worth watching, along with the fable 150+ bucket still showing +7.0% at n=2.
